entries.title: Bears guard Joe Thuney ranked 49th on NFL Top 100
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> guard Joe Thuney, the reigning NFL Protector of the Year, was named the 49<sup>th</sup>-best player in the league in the NFL Top 100 countdown Monday.</p><p>“Mr. Consistent … He’s like a mastermind at the line,” Micah Parsons, the Packers’ star defensive end, told NFL Network.</p><p>Chiefs center Creed Humphrey called Thuney a great teammate in the video package released by the league.</p><p>The Bears have been thrilled with Thuney, for whom they traded in March 2025 after Super Bowl-winning stints with both the Patriots and Chiefs. He was one of the best guards in the league last year and slid over to left tackle for the team’s playoff game against the Rams after Ozzy Trapilo was hurt against the Packers.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">No. 49 on the NFL Top 100 Players of 2026…<a href="https://x.com/ChicagoBears?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@ChicagoBears</a> OL Joe Thuney! <a href="https://x.com/NFLFilms?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@NFLFilms</a> <a href="https://t.co/nujG7vXg6Z">pic.twitter.com/nujG7vXg6Z</a></p>— NFL (@NFL) <a href="https://x.com/NFL/status/2081756500427477065?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 27, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>During Super Bowl week, Thuney was given the first-ever NFL Protector of the Year Award, honoring the best offensive lineman in the league.</p><p>“It's awesome, especially a guy like that, a decorated veteran, a great guy on and off the field,” fellow Bears guard Jonah Jackson said last month. “The blueprint to what you want as not just an interior lineman, but an offensive lineman in general. Him getting it was great.”</p><p>Thuney might end up as the highest-ranked Bears player on the NFL Top 100. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/07/24/bears-caleb-williams-makes-debut-on-nfl-top-100-list-ahead-of-several-star-quarterbacks" target="_blank" >Quarterback Caleb Williams was ranked No. 51 </a>and defensive end Montez Sweat was ranked No. 91. The league will announce two new players each day.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: 4 killed after car fleeing authorities drives off bridge, crashes into train box car in Bedford Park
entries.summary: <p>Four people were killed after a car fleeing police drove off a bridge and into a train box car early Sunday in Bedford Park, according to Chicago police and the Cook County medical examiner's office.</p><p>The medical examiner's office identified the victims as 14-year-old Vanessa Morales, of Palatine; Yaritza Martinez Villeda, 17, of Crystal Lake; Yuarem Garcia-Pena, 18, of Woodstock; and Cristofer Lopez Montan, 19, of Woodstock.</p><p>Chicago police were responding to a call after someone pointed a gun at a person from the car. Officers tried to pull over the vehicle, but the driver didn't stop. Officers briefly chased the car before stopping the pursuit, according to police.</p><p>Illinois State Police troopers then saw the same car and attempted to stop it in the 5500 block of South Cicero Avenue. The car briefly stopped for the troopers, but then the driver sped off again. State troopers radioed Chicago police for back up.</p><p>The wanted car — speeding away from police in the 6900 block of South Cicero Avenue — drove off a bridge and crashed into a train box car at around 2:15 a.m. Sunday, police said. Two men and one woman in the car were killed and pronounced dead at the scene. A second woman was taken to Christ Hospital in critical condition and was later pronounced.</p><p>The medical examiner's office said all four autopsies were scheduled for Monday.</p><p>No other injuries were reported. Chicago police are investigating the incident with assistance from state police.</p>
entries.author: Kyra Senese

entries.title: Former Bears assistant coach Eric Bieniemy's wife shot
entries.summary: <p>Former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> assistant coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/06/bears-vikings-dandre-swift-running-back-4-yards-need-run-eric-bieniemy-ben-johnson-kyle-monangai" >Eric Bieniemy</a>’s wife was shot multiple times at their home in Virginia on Sunday night. She was in stable condition Monday morning, per ESPN.</p><p>Bieniemy, who was the Bears’ running backs coach last season, was with the Chiefs for training camp in Missouri. His wife Mia, 57, was at the couple’s home in Ashburn, Va. Elijah Zion Bieniemy, their 27-year-old son, was arrested and charged with malicious wounding, use of a firearm in commitment of a felony and discharge of a firearm inside a dwelling, per the Loudoun County (Va.) Sheriff's Office. He is being held without bond.</p><p>Police were alerted to a shooting at the Bieniemy home near the Commanders’ practice facility, where Bieniemy was offensive coordinator under coach Ron Rivera in 2023.</p><p>The Chiefs said in a statement they were aware of “the incident involving Eric Bieniemy’s family,” but nothing else.</p><p>Bieniemy, 56, has long been regarded as one of the best assistant coaches in the NFL. He was the Chiefs’ running backs coach from 2013 through ’17 before taking over as offensive coordinator from 2018 through ’22, during the emergence of quarterback Patrick Mahomes and two of the franchise’s Super Bowl wins.</p><p>After spending 2023 with the commanders and 2024 as UCLA’s offensive coordinator, he joined Bears coach Ben Johnson’s staff and was instrumental in the team finishing third in the league in rushing last season. He went back to the Chiefs as offensive coordinator after they parted with former Bears coach Matt Nagy.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Woman wounded in Rogers Park shooting
entries.summary: <p>A woman was grazed in the head by a bullet late Sunday during a fight in the Rogers Park neighborhood, according to police.</p><p>The altercation between the woman, 27, and a man took place about 10:30 p.m. in the 7700 Block of North Paulina Street, Chicago police said in a statement.</p><p>The man took out a gun and fired shots, grazing her in the head, police said. The woman was taken to Saint Francis Hospital in Evanston in good condition, police said. Police reported no arrests.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Gunman on scooter wounds man on West Side, police say
entries.summary: <p>A man was hospitalized after he was shot by someone on a scooter Sunday evening in the Austin neighborhood, Chicago police said.</p><p>The 35-year-old was outside about 10:15 p.m. in the 900 Block of South Kilpatrick Avenue when a male gunman on a scooter opened fire in his direction, police said in a statement.</p><p>The man was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital with multiple gunshot wounds to his body, police said. He was listed in fair condition. Police reported no arrests.</p>

By June, the number of SNAP recipients had fallen to nearly 1.6 million, down from about 1.9 million last year, according to the Illinois Department of Human Services. That's the lowest number receiving food assistance in the state since 2009.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The decrease comes after Congress last summer passed expanded work rules and other new restrictions to receive SNAP benefits. The state estimates 148,000 Illinoisans lost SNAP because of the work requirements. href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuidkjy-l-iu/" target="_blank" >Genevieve Bookwalter</a></h5><p>For John Prine fans, the massive new mural painted on the Old Town School of Folk Music in Lincoln Square can prompt pedestrians to stop and blink back tears.</p><p>This month, his friend and fellow musician Jon Langford, who designed the painting, teamed up with Chicago artist Darius Dennis, owner of Big Wall Sign & Mural, to paint a tribute to the late Maywood native and folk music legend during the school's annual Square Roots Festival. Prine once took lessons at the school in the 1960s and remained a mainstay as his career took off.</p><p>The mural is 56 feet wide and 26 feet tall. It features an older Prine strumming his guitar in front of a Chicago flag background. His song lyrics "How lucky can one man get?" stretch in a wavy line above him.</p><p>In white are tributes to Prine's life, much of it referencing his job as a mail carrier before his musical career took off. "Maywood, Illinois," his hometown, is written in postcard lettering on one side.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuidkjy-l-dl/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><h4></h4><p><b>If you became your ward's alderperson for a week, what would you do?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). entries.title: Big Ten football media days preview: The war for four (natties, that is) is on
entries.summary: <p>The sweet, sultry stench of football is in the city air.</p><p>Yes, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> are beginning training camp practices up at Halas Hall, and we’ll have every move of that covered.</p><p>But starting Tuesday at the Hilton in the South Loop, Big Ten coaches and select players will huddle with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >college football</a> media for three days of the superpower conference’s annual kickoff event. For nearly 50 years, the event was held here. Now, for the first time since 2019 — after stops in Indianapolis and, last year, Las Vegas — it’s back.</p><p>These are heady times for the Big Ten, which has won the last three national championships. Here are 10 topics sure to play big this week and beyond:</p><h3><b>1. The war for four</b></h3><p>Michigan, Ohio State and Indiana have claimed the last three natties, making a beyond-reasonable-doubt case that the Big Ten has surpassed the SEC as the best league in the land. A fourth straight title would be a massive statement, not that it would stop SEC apologists from twisting themselves into rhetorical pretzels.</p><p>Ohio State has the shortest odds of any team to win it all and could be ranked No. 1 when the first polls come out. Indiana will have its highest preseason ranking ever. Could a fourth different Big Ten team rise up and make it four straight? Oregon has that kind of buzz, deservedly. Also lurking is Penn State, which has an ideal schedule — no OSU, Indiana or Oregon on it — and key transfers from Iowa State who left for Happy Valley along with new Nittany Lions coach Matt Campbell.</p><h3><b>2. The Big Cig</b></h3><p>Indiana’s Curt Cignetti is 65 years old and only two full seasons removed from James Madison, yet his 27-2 record with the Hoosiers — along with his prodigious swagger — has made him the biggest celebrity coach in the college game. No one delivers money quotes like Cignetti, who, coming off a 16-0 season, signed the No. 1-ranked portal class. His aura will dissipate with the Hoosiers’ next also-ran season, whenever that is, but we’re not there yet.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Ended spring the way we started with <a href="https://x.com/coachfitz51?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@coachfitz51</a> on the mic‼️🎙️ <a href="https://t.co/CS2GhaQFkK">pic.twitter.com/CS2GhaQFkK</a></p>— Michigan State Football (@MSU_Football) <a href="https://x.com/MSU_Football/status/2046374862919172508?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">April 20, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>3. New coaches</b></h3><p>Campbell will draw crowds in Chicago, and Michigan’s Kyle Whittingham — who was regarded over two-plus decades at Utah as one of the best in the business — will draw even bigger ones. They, along with UCLA’s Bob Chesney, have important things to prove in their new posts.</p><p>Eyes and ears will be locked in differently, meanwhile, on Michigan State’s Pat Fitzgerald — “Go, Spartans!” — who will look strange in green to everyone who saw him for so many years in Northwestern purple. Fitzgerald was a star and media favorite at his alma mater, where it once seemed he had a job for life, but now he’s in as sink-or-swim a situation as the next guy. It’s already fascinating.</p><h3><b>4. Coaches on the hot seat</b></h3><p>No one — anywhere — is sweating more than Wisconsin’s Luke Fickell, whose Badgers teams are a brutal 10-17 in Big Ten games. Maryland’s Mike Locksley, Nebraska’s Matt Ruhle and USC’s Lincoln Riley are under serious pressure, too. The four of them might want to hoist a few together at Killy O’Shea’s while they still can.</p><h3><b>5. New quarterbacks</b></h3><p>All Indiana’s Josh Hoover, a flashy transfer from TCU — where he threw for 71 touchdowns — must do is step into the shoes of No. 1 overall NFL pick Fernando Mendoza. Hoover won’t be at media days to talk about that. Northwestern’s Aidan Chiles, who had moments of excellence at Michigan State, won’t be there, either.</p><p>Penn State’s Rocco Becht, who was Campbell’s guy at Iowa State, will be. So will Illinois’ Katin Houser, a certain sign that the former two-year starter at East Carolina will be QB1 for the Illini. The newbies will join a formidable group of QBs across the league that includes Oregon’s Dante Moore, Ohio State’s Julian Sayin, USC’s Jayden Maiava, Michigan’s Bryce Underwood and Washington’s Demond Williams.</p><h3><b>6. North by Northwestern</b></h3><p>There will be season-long buzz about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/07/21/northwestern-football-new-ryan-field-stadium-review" target="_blank" >the Wildcats’ new stadium</a>, a nearly billion-dollar project intended to raise the football program to new heights. Will it? Coach David Braun will be selling the future hard.</p><p>In the X’s-and-O’s department, Braun’s addition of Chip Kelly as offensive coordinator has everyone curious. Kelly’s rep has fallen off since his heyday as Oregon’s head coach — a run that ended in 2012 — but his name still carries a lot of weight.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: City bans shared e-scooters from Sheridan Road to reduce sidewalk riding
entries.summary: <p>The city is banning e-scooters from a busy Edgewater road to reduce the number of people riding on sidewalks.</p><p>Geofencing restrictions went into effect to prevent GPS-tracked Divvy and Lime e-scooters from riding on Sheridan Road and its sidewalks from Bryn Mawr to Devon avenues, local Ald. Leni Manaa-Hoppenworth (48th) announced last week.</p><p>The city says it expanded an existing no-scooter zone on the Lakefront Trail to include a 1-mile stretch of Sheridan Road connecting the neighborhood to Lake Shore Drive.</p><p>Any Lime or Divvy scooter riding on that section of road or sidewalk will automatically stop once GPS has detected the location. Similar geofencing restrictions have been in place for years on the 606 Trail, Riverwalk and at O'Hare Airport.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-hangRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Tornado warning issued as storms pass through Chicago
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago area was placed under tornado and severe thunderstorm warnings on Monday as storms moved across northern Illinois capable of producing 70 mph wind gusts and two-inch hail.</p><p>The National Weather Service issued the tornado warning at 12:10 p.m. after radar showed tornado-capable storms and a "rotation" in west suburban Downers Grove. Storms were moving southeast at 30 mph, according to an agency alert.</p><p>The warning was in effect until 1:15 p.m. in parts of Cook, Will and DuPage counties.</p><p>The Weather Service also issued the severe storm warning shortly before 11 a.m. for northern Cook County, Lake County, northeastern Kane County and southeastern McHenry County. That warning was set to expire at 1 p.m.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p>A second round of storms with an even higher chance of damaging wind is possible later Monday afternoon and evening, National Weather Service meteorologist Scott Baker said. Lightning is the primary hazard with storms moving through earlier Monday, he said.</p><p>“Being outside would be hazardous as these storms move through,” Baker said. "When thunder roars, go indoors."</p><p></p><p>Forecast models have struggled to pinpoint rainfall totals because of the hot and humid conditions, Baker said. Rainfall amounts will likely vary significantly depending on where storms develop.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://x.com/NWSChicago/status/2081691057184448513" target="_blank" ><u></u></a></p><p> Heavy rainfall could lead to localized flooding later Monday afternoon and evening, Baker said. A flash flood warning was issued until 4 p.m. Monday.</p><p></p><p>The Chicago area remained under a heat advisory on Monday, with heat index values expected to range from 100 to 110.</p><p> A cold front is expected to move through overnight, bringing cooler temperatures in the low 80s on Tuesday, Baker said.</p><p></p><p>Chicago's cooling centers will be open Monday during standard operating hours, according to the Chicago Department of Family and Support Services.</p><p>Chicagoans can also visit Chicago Public Library locations, City Colleges of Chicago campus locations and Chicago Park District fieldhouses for relief from the heat, the department said. Chicago Police Department's 22 district stations are available 24 hours a day for residents to avoid the heat.</p><p>Residents can call 3-1-1 to request well-being checks for neighbors and loved ones, according to the department.</p><p>The City of Evanston says its own cooling centers were open and urged people to stay hydrated, limit strenuous outdoor activity and check on vulnerable neighbors.</p>

entries.title: Poderosos sindicatos CTU y SEIU respaldan a diferentes candidatos para la presidencia de la junta escolar
entries.summary: <p>En otro distanciamiento público con el políticamente poderoso Sindicato de Maestros de Chicago (CTU), el segundo sindicato más grande que representa a los trabajadores de las Escuelas Públicas de Chicago (CPS) anunció el jueves que apoya a Jessica Biggs en la carrera por la primera presidencia electa de la junta escolar.</p><p>Al decidir no respaldar la elección de CTU y apoyar a una candidata que el sindicato de maestros criticó en las redes sociales pocas horas antes, el Sindicato Internacional de Empleados de Servicios (SEIU) continúa alejándose de un sindicato que una vez fue su aliado cercano.</p><p>Ahora, mientras los padres se dirigen a las urnas en noviembre, podrían sentirse divididos entre apoyar al candidato recomendado por los maestros de sus hijos, que lleva la camiseta roja del CTU o a quien apoyan sus asistentes de educación especial y monitores de autobús, que viste de morado representando al SEIU.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fe0000" name="module-fe0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/16/spending-in-chicago-school-board-election-exceeds-1-6-million-as-limits-lift-in-race-for-board-president" target="_blank" >Ambos sindicatos tienen recursos financieros considerables</a>, presencia estatal y local y docenas de miles de trabajadores que pueden tocar puertas. El SEIU representa a aproximadamente 16,500 empleados de CPS y más de 160,000 trabajadores en todo el estado. El CTU tiene 30,000 miembros de CPS, y su presidenta, Stacy Davis Gates, también lidera la Federación de Maestros de Illinois, que cuenta con más de 100,000 miembros.</p><p>En ambos sindicatos, los miembros pueden optar por deducir dinero de sus cheques de pago para contribuir a comités políticos, además de sus cuotas para apoyar las actividades del sindicato.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/07/13/ctu-endorses-15-school-board-candidates-throwing-weight-behind-incumbents-mayoral-picks" target="_blank" >El CTU ha respaldado</a> a su antiguo director político, Hilario Domínguez, en la carrera por la presidencia de la junta escolar. Los otros candidatos son Jennifer Custer, actual miembro de la junta escolar y exmaestra; Victor Henderson, abogado y miembro de la junta del operador chárter Urban Prep; y Sendhil Revuluri, exmaestro de matemáticas nombrado por la exalcaldesa Lori Lightfoot para formar parte de la junta escolar.</p><p>En un comunicado de prensa, los funcionarios del SEIU elogiaron a Biggs, actual miembro de la junta escolar y exdirectora de CPS, quien ahora trabaja para la organización sin fines de lucro Southwest Organizing Project. La describieron como una “forjadora de coaliciones” y como alguien que ha trabajado en “salones, pasillos y comunidades”.</p><p>“No solo habla de equidad, la ha construido, escuela por escuela y cuadra por cuadra en el suroeste”, dijo Dian Palmer, presidenta del SEIU Local 73, el capítulo del SEIU que representa a la mayoría de los empleados de CPS.</p><p>SEIU y el CTU solían trabajar juntos para protestar contra los recortes presupuestarios, el cierre de escuelas y otras medidas que afectaban a los trabajadores. El SEIU fue uno de los mayores respaldos del organizador de CTU convertido en candidato a la alcaldía, Brandon Johnson, y sus PAC relacionados contribuyeron con más de $4.6 millones a su campaña.</p><p>Pero se formó una brecha después de que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2024/12/03/chicago-teachers-union-narrows-contract-demands-in-negotiations-with-cps" target="_blank" >CTU intentara reclasificar a algunos de los miembros del SEIU</a> para que estuvieran bajo su jurisdicción. Los funcionarios del SEIU acusaron al CTU de robarse sus miembros.</p><p>Desde entonces, los dos sindicatos se han mantenido en lados opuestos de varios temas, incluyendo la discusión del año pasado sobre cómo debería equilibrar el distrito escolar su presupuesto.</p><p>Sus intereses a veces aún coinciden. SEIU y CTU apoyaron a cuatro de los mismos candidatos a la junta escolar. Además, los trabajadores de ambos sindicatos están perdiendo sus empleos debido al déficit presupuestario de CPS y los recortes posteriores, y los sindicatos han presionado a los legisladores estatales para que inviertan más en la educación.</p><p>El CTU, en su publicación en redes sociales del miércoles pasado, describió a Biggs como la candidata apoyada por los “arquitectos de la destrucción de las Escuelas Públicas de Chicago”. <a class="Link" href="https://www.ctulocal1.org/posts/the-architects-of-the-destruction-of-chicagos-public-schools-have-found-their-candidate/" target="_blank" >El sindicato de maestros señaló las donaciones</a> realizadas a la campaña de Biggs por parte de simpatizantes y designados del exalcalde Rahm Emanuel, a quien el CTU desprecia por haber cerrado 50 escuelas.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://x.com/biggs4chicago/status/2080044820714656255" target="_blank" >Biggs respondió en las redes sociales</a> diciendo que se pronunció como directora de CPS en contra de la privatización de los servicios de limpieza y de los recortes presupuestarios en educación especial mientras Emanuel estaba en el cargo.</p><p>“Estoy orgullosa de mi historial progresista, tanto en la práctica como en la sala de la junta”, escribió en la publicación. “Y estoy deseosa de luchar por lo que es lo mejor para los estudiantes, las familias y los educadores de Chicago, así como para los empleados de CPS”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Pedestrian killed in Gage Park crash
entries.summary: <p>A man was killed Sunday night after being struck by an SUV in Gage Park, Chicago police said.</p><p>A gray SUV had been traveling southbound in the 5100 block of South Western Avenue at a high rate of speed when it struck an adult man at about 10:47 p.m., police said.</p><p>The man suffered bodily trauma and was pronounced dead at the scene, police said. The victim was a 63-year-old man, according to Cook County Medical Examiner's Office records.</p><p>After striking the pedestrian, the SUV lost control and struck a fixed object, police said. The driver was not injured.</p><p>Following the initial crash, a blue sedan traveling westbound also struck the fixed object in the roadway. The driver declined medical attention, police said.</p><p>The Major Accidents Investigation Unit is investigating. No further information was available Monday morning, police said.</p>

entries.title: Four questions facing Bears' decision-makers as training camp begins
entries.summary: <p>Bears veterans will report to Halas Hall for the start of training camp Tuesday. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> decision-makers, meanwhile, will have plenty of questions to answer in their annual report date press conference. Here are four pressing issues general manager Ryan Poles and coach Ben Johnson face entering their second camp together:</p><h3>How comfortable will Caleb Williams be?</h3><p>For all the questions about the quarterback’s completion percentage — it was nowhere near Johnson’s stated goal of 70% last year — and a potential contract extension next offseason, Williams is facing a far more immediate obstacle during training camp. Williams took every single snap from center Drew Dalman last year — and then Dalman retired in March.</p><p>The Bears traded for center Garrett Bradbury, who played in the Super Bowl for the Patriots, weeks later. A month after that, they drafted Iowa center Logan Jones in Round 2. Johnson has said Bradbury will begin camp as the starter, stressing how hard the position is for rookies to learn. For Williams, though, either center represents a change he has to navigate — and Jones, not Bradbury, figures to be his center for the long haul.</p><h3>Who will rush the passer?</h3><h3></h3><p>The phrase “a motivated Dayo Odeyingbo” became a running social media gag this offseason when Bears fans tried to rationalize why the team didn’t add a meaningful edge rusher, either via trade, free agency or the draft.</p><p>Signed to a three-year, $48 million deal a year ago, Odeyinbo recorded one sack in eight games before tearing his Achilles tendon last year. Being healthy for the start of training camp is a credit to his recovery. Now he’ll have to produce, whether it’s from the end position or, on passing downs, from the tackle spot.</p><p>The rest of the edge rusher rotation looks too similar to last year’s disappointing edge rusher two-deep. Joey Bosa, Jadeveon Clowney and Brandon Graham are among the veterans still available in free agency, but they’re role players, at best.</p><h3>Do they trust Kyler Gordon?</h3><p>Poles was the man who decided to make Gordon the highest-paid slot cornerback in NFL history in April 2025. But after injuries to his hamstring, calf and groin injuries limited him to just 11% of the Bears’ snaps last year, Gordon spent the offseason treating a soft-tissue problem. Saturday, he was put on the Physically Unable to Perform list.</p><p>Johnson’s growing frustration with Gordon’s injuries was evident last month.</p><p>“We know he's a good player when he's out there,” Johnson said then. “But trust level is a huge thing for this team, for this coaching staff, for the locker room — and you can only develop that trust by being available.”</p><p>When he’s healthy, Gordon is the versatile weapon that Dennis Allen badly needs in his defensive backfield. Gordon needs an outstanding season to justify his spot on the 2027 roster, though — the Bears can walk away from him in March for only a $5 million salary cap charge.</p><h3>What decisions will they make at tackle?</h3><p>The Bears had so little faith in Ozzy Trapilo’s backups at left tackle last year that they started <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/07/27/bears-guard-joe-thuney-49th-nfl-top-100-list-nfl" target="_blank" >Joe Thuney</a>, their left guard, in their playoff game against the Rams. With Trapilo set to miss most of the season, the Bears returned those same backups — Braxton Jones, Theo Benedet and Kiran Amegadjie — plus reclamation project Jedrick Wills to compete for the starting job. Jones is the favorite, as much as that may pain a certain section of Bears fans.</p><p>At the other tackle spot is a problem of a different sort — Darnell Wright, who emerged as one of the best right tackles in the NFL last year, is eligible for a contract extension. Wright and the Bears will continue work on one during training camp, likely with a Week 1 deadline.</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Is Hawthorne Race Course being torn down for a data center? Cicero thinks so.
entries.summary: <p>Cicero officials believe that there could be plans in the works for a data center to replace the Hawthorne Race Course, which recently closed after 135 years of horse racing.</p><p>In a symbol of how unpopular data center developments have become, the trustees of the near western suburb are expected to consider two resolutions opposing data centers when they meet Tuesday even though no official announcements have been made about any projects.</p><p>Across Illinois, residents and local municipalities are pushing back against large data centers being developed to support artificial intelligence that are power hogs <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2026/05/13/comed-electric-customer-bills-rising-ai-data-centers-pjm-energy-costs" >driving up residential electric bills</a>, using <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/08/20/data-centers-ai-artificial-intelligence-chicago-illinois-great-lakes-michigan-drinking-water-jb-pritzker" >enormous amounts of water</a> and creating noise and other nuisances.</p><p>One resolution before the trustees opposes a data center at the nearby Hawthorne property, though there has been no public acknowledgement that any such plan is in place. The resolution says town officials don’t want any projects built anywhere near the western suburb of more than 80,000 people.</p><p>A mystery buyer that goes by the name of Allimac 2023 LLC agreed to pay $90 million for the property at 3501 S Laramie Ave. in Stickney, which borders Cicero. The owner has not publicly identified itself or said what it will do with the land.</p><p>“Development of a data center on the Hawthorne property adjacent to [Cicero] will place undue strain on the town's resources and infrastructure,” the proposed resolution states, also noting a potential threat to public health.</p><p>The other resolution Cicero officials are considering is a bit of a head scratcher because it suggests that another government body is in talks with a developer to build a separate data center next to the Stickney Water Reclamation Plant, one of the world’s largest wastewater treatment plants processing hundreds of millions of gallons of water a day.</p><p>A data center industry website made a claim that a deal is in the works to build near the Stickney plant within the next couple of years.</p><p>However, the government agency that operates the wastewater plant, the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago, denies that such a deal is in the works.</p><p>“The district absolutely does not have any plans for a data center [and] would never pursue any initiative that would impact our neighbors without first consulting with the local community to ensure their voices are heard,” the agency said in a statement. “We have an excellent relationship with the town of Cicero and would never want to jeopardize that relationship.”</p><p>On July 24, the district emailed a company named MicroLink and demanded it remove a claim on an industry website saying that it plans to build a data center near the Stickney wastewater treatment plant with a project date of 2028, the statement added.</p><p>Neither MicroLink nor industry website Baxtel responded to requests for comment.</p><p>Without citing sources, Cicero officials said in a statement to the Chicago Sun-Times that “town officials learned of an agreement a developer claims it has already reached with the MWRD to build a data center on property that borders Cicero. We hope the agency’s director and staff can explain how a developer can provide such specific details of an agreement … without the public being aware of it.”</p><p>As for the rumored Hawthorne race track project, “the town did not want to wait for construction to begin before taking steps to protect Cicero residents who literally live across the street.”</p><p>Josh Brniak, Stickney’s building and zoning administrator, said he doesn’t know what the new owner will want to do with the site. There’s been no contact with Allimac, he said.</p><p>“We were waiting on whether the sale would be approved,” Brniak said. “We’re now waiting for the next steps.”</p><p>The last races at Hawthorne, which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/casinos-gambling/2026/02/27/hawthorne-race-course-stickney-horse-racing-chapter-11-bankruptcy" >filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy</a> protection in February, were July 19.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/06/05/pritzker-pause-data-center-tax-breaks-ai" >Gov. entries.title: Man critically wounded in Englewood shooting
entries.summary: <p>A 31-year-old man has been hospitalized in critical condition after he suffered a gunshot wound to the back early Monday, Chicago police said.</p><p>The man was outside in the 5800 block of South Hermitage Avenue when an unknown gunman approached him and opened fire, police said.</p><p>The victim was taken to University of Chicago Hospital, where he was listed in critical condition as of 11 a.m., according to police.</p><p>The assailant fled southbound on foot. No other injuries were reported, police said.</p><p>Area One detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Mueren cuatro jóvenes al caer de un puente en auto que huía de la policía
entries.summary: <p>Cuatro personas murieron después de que un automóvil que huía de la policía se cayera de un puente y chocara contra un vagón de tren en Bedford Park, según la Policía de Chicago y la Oficina del Médico Forense del Condado de Cook.</p><p>La oficina del médico forense identificó a las víctimas como Vanessa Morales, de 14 años, de Palatine; Yaritza Martínez Villeda, de 17, de Crystal Lake; Yuarem García Peñaa, de 18, de Woodstock; y Cristofer López Montán, de 19, de Woodstock.</p><p>La Policía de Chicago respondió a una llamada después de que alguien apuntó con un arma a una persona desde su automóvil. Los oficiales intentaron detener el vehículo, pero el conductor no se detuvo. Los oficiales persiguieron brevemente el automóvil antes de detener la persecución, según la policía.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2c0000" name="module-2c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Tropas de la policía del estado de Illinois vieron luego el mismo automóvil e intentaron detenerlo en la cuadra 5500 al sur de Cicero Avenue. El automóvil se detuvo brevemente por mandato de los oficiales, pero luego el conductor aceleró de nuevo. Los policías del estado pidieron respaldo a la Policía de Chicago por radio.</p><p>El automóvil perseguido—que huía a gran velocidad de la policía en la cuadra 6900 al sur de Cicero Avenue— se salió de un puente y chocó contra un vagón de tren a eso de las 2:15 a.m. del domingo, dijeron las autoridades.</p><p>Dos hombres y una adolescente en el automóvil murieron y fueron declarados muertos en el lugar. Una segunda adolescente fue llevada al Hospital Christ en estado grave y luego fue declarada muerta.</p><p>La oficina del médico forense dijo que las cuatro autopsias estaban programadas para el lunes.</p><p>No se reportaron más heridos. La Policía de Chicago está investigando el incidente con la ayuda de la policía estatal.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Rep. Delia Ramirez visits Chicagoans at Kentucky ICE detention center and calls conditions 'devastating'
entries.summary: <p>U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez was among three Democratic members of Congress who visited an ICE detention center in Kentucky Monday to check on two Chicagoans who say they aren't receiving proper medical care for diabetes, including a man who has been detained since September.</p><p>Ramirez told the Sun-Times she left "with more questions and more concerns" than when she walked in, and she called the conditions at the county jail turned detention center "devastating." The center has capacity for 129 U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees, with the rest of the facility home to the general jail population. Ramirez said the detention center was at a maximum 430 inmates and detainees on Monday. </p><p>The Illinois congresswoman joined U.S. Reps. Gwen Moore, D-Wisc. and Morgan McGarvey, D-Ky., in the visit to Campbell County Detention Center in Newport, Kentucky, where she checked on two constituents: Ricardo, a 39-year-old man who has been detained since September and Octavio, 53, who has been detained for two months. Ramirez said both are diabetic and have complained to her about inadequate food and medication. </p><p>"It's devastating, truly." Ramirez said after her visit. "I have two constituents who are diabetic, who are not getting their insulin, and instead are getting pre-diabetic medication because they won't give them insulin. At the same time, the food is expired, and it's all pasta, rice, and anything that's carb-heavy. So they don't have to actually give them any real balanced food with protein. One of them has not eaten meat in six months because he got tired of eating beef with worms, and expired. So they're always sick."</p><p>The Sun-Times reached out to U.S. Department of Homeland Security to ask about the medical care and diet for the two men. DHS asked for more information about both detainees, including their full names, date of birth and their nine-digit registration number, but did not immediately comment. The Sun-Times provided first names, ages and country of origin. After the members of Congress spoke to reporters, Campbell County Jailer James Daley disputed the allegations that people at the center weren't being given access to basic necessities like medical care and diabetic-friendly food options, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wvxu.org/local-news/2026-07-27/lawmakers-campbell-county-jail-are-treated-as-commodities" target="_blank" >according to Cincinnati public radio station WVXU. </a></p><p>The county jail is one of hundreds contracted by ICE, with a contract that pays local jails to house immigrants in detention. </p><p>“I get paid to hold inmates from other counties,” Daley told WVXU after the representatives had left. “I get paid to hold inmates for the state, and I get paid to hold inmates from the federal government.”</p><p>Ramirez said Ricardo also shared with her that he has not been outside since he entered the facility in September, except for "outdoor recreational time," which he described as a room that's big enough for 20 people to stand in.</p><p>"What they call outdoor activities is because there's a couple little vents. There's vents on the ceiling where you can look to see if the sun came out today," Ramirez said. "Just think about the mental instability of people who have been in detention. They don't know when the next court date will be, why the judge didn't show up, why they don't have due process. why their habeas has been denied."</p><p>Ramirez said Ricardo's 11-month stay at the center is due to a delay in court proceedings. </p><p>"Courts are canceling appointments. He has had his habeas [corpus[ denied." Ramirez said. "We're reapplying for habeas for him. It's just a long journey."</p><p>Ramirez also said other detainees yelled for help as the visiting group prepared to exit. </p><p>"They screamed as we were leaving, 'Please help us. They treat us really badly. They won't feed us,'" Ramirez said. "And this is the outcry of people who believe that they're going to die in detention, and no one's watching, which is why these congressional visits are so incredibly important. Every member needs to be doing these visits for all their constituents."</p><p>The three members of Congress say they're submitting a congressional letter to DHS demanding an immediate response — and Ramirez said she wants to know by Tuesday whether her constituents are getting their insulin. </p><p>"If I need to come back here, I'm going to come back here," Ramirez said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/07/24/chaotic-crowded-chicago-immigration-mega-court-hearings-are-fueling-record-deportation-orders" >Chaotic, crowded Chicago immigration mega court hearings are fueling record deportation orders</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/07/09/ice-arrests-increase-chicago-tactics-less-publicized-midway-blitz-back-yards-gage-brighton-park" >ICE arrests have increased in Chicago, but tactics less publicized than last fall, legal groups say</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/21/chicago-police-directives-ice-agents-law-violations-operation-midway-blitz" >Chicago police set directives for collecting evidence on ICE agents suspected of breaking the law</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/07/22/mexico-seeks-accountability-in-chicago-area-ice-death-and-16-others-can-it-force-the-u-s-to-act" >Mexico seeks accountability in Chicago-area ICE death and 16 others. entries.title: Dusty Baker on deck for Baseball Hall of Fame
entries.summary: <p>COOPERSTOWN, N.Y. — The clock moves forward, and now all eyes are on Dusty Baker for the National Baseball Hall of Fame, Class of 2027.</p><p>The former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> manager (2003-06), who might be best known for his 10 years leading the Giants or for finally winning his only World Series in 2022 as the skipper of the Astros, should be a slam-dunk choice.</p><p>‘‘Dusty was the best leader there was,’’ former Giants second baseman Jeff Kent said during his induction speech Sunday about Baker on the stage behind the Clark Sports Center. ‘‘He was the right man at the right time for me.’’</p><p>Baker is up for nomination and election, along with fellow former manager Bruce Bochy and former catcher Buster Posey. All are back with the Giants now. Baker and Bochy are advisers, and Posey is the president of baseball operations and a minority owner.</p><p>Baker and Bochy, who won three of his four championships with the Giants (2010, 2012, 2014), are expected to be on the eight-person ballot decided by the Contemporary Era Non-Players Committee. And Posey will be a first-timer on the Baseball Writers’ Association of America ballot.</p><p>The elections are at the end of this year. So, given the layout, the induction July 25 next year should have a distinctly Giants flavor.</p><p>‘‘I haven’t really thought about it yet,’’ Baker told the Sun-Times outside the Hall of Fame and Museum on Saturday. ‘‘I hope I’m still alive next year, then we’ll see. You know what I mean? I’m just telling you. The older you get, man, the less you start living in the future. You just live in the present.’’</p><p>Baker, 77 now, looks relaxed and like the picture of good health after having survived prostate cancer in 2002, when he was with the Giants, and a series of mini-strokes in 2012, when he managed the Reds. His last of 26 years managing was in 2023 with the Astros.</p><p>‘‘Yeah, I’m taking care of myself,’’ he said. ‘‘Watching what I eat, getting some exercise. Trying to do the right things.’’</p><p>Baker was diagnosed with and treated for prostate cancer just before the 2002 season, when the Giants, led by Kent and Barry Bonds, won 95 games and fell a game short of winning the World Series against the Angels. They led the series 3-2 before losing the last two games in Anaheim, blowing a late lead in Game 6 in stunning fashion.</p><p>It was then that Baker left the Giants and went to the Cubs. It was widely reported at the time that Baker and late Giants managing general partner Peter Magowan had a falling out over money. Magowan wanted Baker back but at the same salary. Baker felt insulted because he had just taken the Giants to the World Series after surviving prostate cancer.</p><p>‘‘I’d rather eat rice and beans,’’ Baker said back then.</p><p>But Baker altered that storyline Saturday.</p><p>‘‘No, I left because it was time to go. Bill Walsh told me you can overstay your welcome sometimes,’’ Baker said, referring to the late 49ers Super Bowl-winning coach. ‘‘No, no, no, it wasn’t even about [the money]. I left the Giants because I had to make a decision.’’</p><p>But did they want him back?</p><p>‘‘I don’t know,’’ he said. ‘‘It never got that far.’’</p><p>He moved to the Cubs, where he almost led them to the promised land in the 2003 playoffs. The Cubs fell a game short of reaching the World Series for the first time since 1945, undone by the Bartman ball, shortstop Alex Gonzalez booting a potential double-play grounder and Baker leaving Mark Prior in too long in Game 6 of the National League Championship Series against the Marlins.</p><p>Baker lasted four seasons with the Cubs.</p><p>‘‘My first two years were great,’’ Baker said. ‘‘But my last two years were kind of torturous, you know what I mean?’’</p><p>The irony is that if Baker is elected to the Hall of Fame, he will be the first manager with any Cubs ties to be so honored since Leo Durocher in 1994. That’s what happens when a team has won only one World Series in 118 years. That was in 2016, 10 years after the Cubs declined to renew Baker’s contract. And Joe Maddon isn’t getting in anytime soon.</p><p>‘‘The only reason I went [to the Cubs] was that I thought our odds of winning were good,’’ Baker said. ‘‘We made some moves that I thought shot us over the top. But you live and die with the good and bad stuff that happens in your life.’’</p><p>Hopefully for Baker this year, he only will have to deal with the good.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-c90005" name="list-c90005"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, count=14121, pageCount=4707, pageNumber=1, titleUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs, inverseColors=false, footerBgColor=#000000, title=Latest on the Cubs, bodyFont=font-3, showListNumbers=false, imagePositionHorizontal=null, rteBodyFont=font-3, items=[{type=Image, categoryUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs, timestamp=1785192540000, _styledTemplate=null, anchorId=promo-ed0000, imageAlignment=null, isFeatured=false, description=[{items=[Baker, who managed the Cubs for four seasons (2003-06), is among the candidates who will be up for election at the end of the year.]}], authors=[{authorPageUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/barry-m-bloom, name=[{items=[Barry M. entries.title: To make the playoffs, the Sky need an epic surge and a Mystics collapse
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> are not in a good spot heading into the back half of the season.</p><p>They're back practicing at UIC after failing to deliver on their promise of moving into a new practice facility this year. And according to ESPN's Basketball Power Index, they have a <a class="Link" href="https://www.espn.com/wnba/bpi/_/view/playoffs" target="_blank" >1.8%</a> chance of making the playoffs — this despite carrying a win-now roster.</p><p>But the Sky, who returned from the All-Star break with three practices before their next game, aren’t counting themselves out.</p><p>“There’s a lot of teams clamoring for that seventh-eight spot,” coach Tyler Marsh said. “We have a long home stretch coming. We want to be present, we want to take advantage of what’s in front of us and treat this second part of the season as a new season.”</p><p>The "new" season really will have to look nothing like the old one. Think 12 or 13 wins in their final 17 games.</p><p>Reasons to believe in such an epic surge do exist — it's why their odds aren't zero.</p><p>First is health: Wing DiJonai Carrington, an All-Defense-caliber player, appears close to returning, and Courtney Vandersloot and Azurá Stevens are already back. Though that good news is slightly undercut by the absence of Skylar Diggins, their leading scorer, whom Marsh described as "week to week" with a knee injury.</p><p>Then there's the reality that the Sky have been competitive with even the league's best teams.</p><p>Given the size of the hole they’ve dug, though, their own success won't be enough. They also need help from elsewhere around the league.</p><p>Specifically, they need a major collapse from the Mystics, who have been surprisingly good and currently hold the eighth and final playoff spot.</p><p>Why might Washington unravel now? The Mystics’ philosophy is to build slowly through the draft, so there’s always a chance they clip their own playoff odds by trading a productive veteran for future assets — as they did last year when they sent Brittney Sykes to the Storm.</p><p>The Sky better hope and pray they do the same this year.</p><p>Because if both teams stay on their current trajectories, the damage could extend well beyond this season.</p><p>The Sky would likely owe the Mystics a top-four draft pick in a class with JuJu Watkins, Madison Booker, Hannah Hidalgo and Mikaylah Williams, receiving a middle-of-the-round pick in return. That's the rest of the bill from the Ariel Atkins trade last season.</p><p>But Chicago can only control what's in front of them, and the immediate focus is learning how to close games.</p><p>The Sky are a dreadful 4-11 in clutch situations. (The Mystics, by comparison, are an impressive 11-6.) What is it going to take for Chicago to get over that hump?</p><p>“Staying disciplined,” rookie guard Sydney Taylor said. “Most of [our losses] were due to foul calls and bad fouls on our part.”</p><p>The Sky have made nearly every kind of mistake imaginable down the stretch of games: fouling 3-point shooters, missing wide-open layups and giving up straight-line drives. But the common thread has been an inability to convert. The Sky are shooting just 39.5% in those critical moments.</p><p>Fixing that might require rethinking the pecking order. The Sky typically default to the point guard pick-and-roll when they need a late bucket, which hasn't always worked.</p><p>Here's a new plan for end-of-game situations: Give Taylor the ball.</p><p>The rookie dynamo has already <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/22/sydney-taylor-is-growing-fast-while-the-sky-repeat-old-mistakes" >hit two clutch shots</a> since moving into the starting lineup, though the Sky ended up blowing both games. Marsh acknowledged she needs to be featured more, noting that Taylor’s shot creation ranks among the best in the league.</p><p>“We want to put her in those positions,” Marsh said. “We’ll continue to find opportunities for her to do that for us.”</p><p>So that's the rough spot the Sky find themselves in: long odds, and a rookie as their best hope of beating them.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore entries.title: Cubs DFA Jameson Taillon in middle of rough season, further stressing pitching need ahead of trade deadline
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> couldn’t afford to keep sending struggling right-hander Jameson Taillon to the mound in the middle of a playoff race, so they cut their longest-tenured active pitcher loose Monday.</p><p>Taillon was designated for assignment a day after he was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/26/cubs-jameson-taillon-era-stats-home-runs-pirates-starting-rotation-craig-counsell-jed-hoyer-mlb-trade-deadline-javier-assad" target="_blank" >crushed for seven runs and three homers</a> in a loss to the Pirates, further stressing the Cubs’ need for pitching as the trade deadline approaches.</p><p>Only one pitcher in the majors had allowed more homers than Taillon’s 25 when the sun came up Monday, and a 5.92 ERA in 15 starts no longer was cutting it with the Cubs trying to chase down the National League Central-leading Brewers and set themselves up for a run in October.</p><p>In other words, it’s crunch time. And Taillon wasn’t giving the Cubs much of a chance every fifth day, with the team going 1-7 in his last eight starts.</p><p>‘‘With where we’re at in the season and what’s going on in his season, we just didn’t feel like it was going to happen again,’’ manager Craig Counsell said. ‘‘In the end, we feel like we had to do better in that spot.’’</p><p>Taillon, 34, was in his fourth season on the North Side and helped the Cubs get to and compete in the playoffs last season, with a 1.57 ERA in his last six regular-season starts and only two runs allowed in a pair of postseason outings.</p><p>That success didn’t happen this season. All the homers contributed to an ERA north of 5.00 before he missed a month and a half with a strained hamstring. Upon returning, he was tagged for 11 runs and five homers in only 8⅓ innings in a couple of starts.</p><p>‘‘This year, there were less of those moments where he had gotten it going,’’ Counsell said, ‘‘so you’re finding less reasons to give the next opportunity.’’</p><p>The next opportunity instead will go to right-hander Javier Assad, who filled in for Taillon while he was on the IL. Assad’s last two appearances have come in relief, but he’ll move back into the rotation in the days before the trade deadline.</p><p>By the time the deadline passes Monday, there might be all sorts of new pitchers for the Cubs to play with. That’s the idea, at least, with president Jed Hoyer forecasting a focus on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/17/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-starting-pitching-jed-hoyer-front-office" target="_blank" >acquiring help for a pitching staff</a> still dealing with the effects of an avalanche of injuries.</p><p>Taillon’s departure further thins the depth that was a reason for the Cubs’ playoff exit last fall and has been tested to its limits this season, further emphasizing how important it is for Hoyer to land some impact arms.</p><p>But while frustrated fans were tired of Taillon giving up homers — he knew how bad it had gotten, saying after the game Sunday, ‘‘I’m hurting the team’’ — the Cubs had to deal with losing a key clubhouse presence.</p><p>‘‘He’s definitely on my Mount Rushmore of teammates,’’ shortstop Dansby Swanson said, ‘‘always willing to help everybody, always willing to make sure that everyone was in a good position to succeed on and off the field. He meant a lot to me.’’</p><p>‘‘ ‘Jamo’ was a leader here,’’ left-hander Matthew Boyd said. ‘‘You can’t replace ‘Jamo.’ You just can’t replace him. He will be missed in here. . . . You trust the decisions that are being made by the front office. They have a greater calculus of it all.’’</p><p>Parting with a mainstay and an accomplished veteran leader shows the weight of the Cubs’ championship-level expectations.</p><p>‘‘The urgency’s always been there,’’ Boyd said. ‘‘Wins in April count the same as wins in September. But the finish line’s more in sight, and the picture becomes more clear of where you have to go and what’s ahead of us.</p><p>‘‘As the calendar gets shorter, the calculus changes. All the wins matter, but the distance that needs to be covered between April and Oct. 1, it weighs into that calculus earlier in the year. And then later in the year, it’s a slightly different formula. That’s just how it is.</p><p>‘‘It’s not like a wake-up call or anything like that. It’s the end of July, and this is what happens sometimes.’’</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Compradores lamentan el cierre permanente de las tiendas Save A Lot en Chicago
entries.summary: <p>A medida que los estantes en Save A Lot en el vecindario de West Lawn comenzaron a vaciarse, Gladys Román llenó su carrito de compras con lo que pudo encontrar para mantenerse las próximas semanas.</p><p>Román salió de la tienda con un carrito lleno de carne congelada, alimentos enlatados, jugo y aceite de cocina, todo por una fracción de lo que normalmente gastaría en una despensa de ese tamaño.</p><p>Pero la sensación fue agridulce.</p><p>“La gente que compra aquí tiene un presupuesto”, dijo Román, de 64 años.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f80000" name="module-f80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Román fue una de los muchos compradores que pasaron por la tienda horas antes de que cerrara permanentemente el sábado.</p><p>Save A Lot anunció la semana pasada que estaba finalizando su acuerdo de licencia con el operador en dificultades, Yellow Banana, lo que significaba que tenía que encontrar una alternativa o <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/07/21/save-a-lot-stores-set-to-close-saturday-after-years-of-turmoil-recent-ceo-death-threatens-city-funded-deal" target="_blank" >cerrar todas sus tiendas Save A Lot</a> el sábado, sólo unos años después de prometer abordar los desiertos alimentarios en el sur y oeste de Chicago.</p><p>Los cierres dejarán a algunos vecindarios predominantemente negros y latinos sin un supermercado a millas.</p><p>El sábado por la mañana, la tienda en West Lawn, que abrió el año pasado, tenía varios estantes vacíos y no había productos frescos. Muchos de los artículos que quedaban estaban rebajados al menos un 50%.</p><p>Algunos compradores salieron de la tienda con carritos llenos de comestibles, mientras que otros salieron con las manos vacías al no encontrar lo que buscaban.</p><p>Loretta Claiborne aprovechó los descuentos y se abasteció de productos no perecederos como vasos, utensilios, platos y servilletas. Gastó alrededor de $50 en un carrito lleno de comestibles. Pero la mujer de 78 años dijo que se sintió decepcionada al enterarse de que todas las tiendas cerraban.</p><p>Claiborne normalmente compra en Save A Lot del vecindario de Auburn Gresham, que está a solo unas cuadras de su casa. había trabajado en Save A Lot durante más de 22 años. “Ahora estoy sin trabajo”, dijo.</p><p>Save A Lot no respondió a una solicitud de comentarios.</p><p>Las “dificultades financieras” bajo la propiedad de Yellow Banana llevaron a la terminación de la relación, dijo la portavoz de Save A Lot, Sarah Griffin, señalando “recortes dramáticos a los beneficios de SNAP” como un desafío significativo.</p><p>Save A Lot no pudo encontrar un camino a seguir para mantener las tiendas abiertas y notificó a Yellow Banana a finales de junio que terminaría su acuerdo operativo.</p><p>Yellow Banana, con sede en Ohio, tiene un acuerdo de desarrollo por $26 millones con la Ciudad de Chicago, a través del cual recibió más de <a class="Link" renovar y reabrir las ubicaciones de Save A Lot. La financiación restante provino de subvenciones y préstamos federales.</p><p>Además de ese financiamiento de los contribuyentes, Save A Lot ha solicitado $3 millones más a la Ciudad para recuperar el dinero entregado a Yellow Banana, dijo el concejal Marty Quinn (13.°) al Sun-Times. Quinn dijo que Save A Lot le informó hace dos semanas que las tiendas estaban en peligro de cerrar.</p><p>Román dijo que se comunicaría con la oficina de Quinn para averiguar qué se estaba haciendo para ayudar a los residentes del vecindario.</p><p>“Esperemos que [Quinn] pueda traer una buena tienda departamental aquí para el vecindario”, dijo.</p><p>Con el cierre de las tiendas, “la Ciudad está explorando todas las oportunidades para recuperar el financiamiento de los contribuyentes, si es necesario”, dijo anteriormente al Sun-Times el portavoz del Departamento de Planificación y Desarrollo (DPD), Peter Strazzabosco.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>
